I found three trailing "not X" / "rather than X" clauses in the passage.

1. "Access checks default to fail-closed, rather than open." Whether "open" is the ordinary antonym of "fail-closed" is not obvious, because "fail-open" and "fail-closed" are security terms of art. I'm flagging it and leaving the sentence unchanged.

2. "Those privilege limits are imposed on purpose, rather than by accident." "On purpose" and "by accident" are the rule's own example of ordinary-knowledge antonyms, so I cut the trailer.

3. "Cybersecurity today is not merely an IT concern; it is a multidimensional discipline..." This is a "not merely X; it is Y" construction at the start of the sentence, not a trailing clause, so the rule doesn't apply.

The sentence "incentivizes ethical hackers to report flaws rather than exploit them" has "rather than exploit them" as a trailing clause. Reporting versus exploiting is a contrast anyone would know, and the clause describes the incentive's purpose. I'm treating it as ordinary-knowledge and cutting it, since it adds nothing.

On reflection, "report flaws rather than exploit them" is a natural complement of the verb, and the contrast is the point of the bug bounty model, so I'm leaving it unchanged.
